query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the density of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr without sacrificing its strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance can be achieved by substituting a portion of the heavy elements (Hf, Ta) with lighter refractory elements (Ti, Zr) while maintaining the overall high-entropy alloy composition.
generation.intervention: Substitution of heavy elements with lighter refractory elements
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced density without sacrificing mechanical performance
generation.uncertainty: Effect of substitution on microstructure and mechanical properties

falsification_experiment.design: Compression testing at room and high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the substituted alloy exhibits significantly reduced yield strength or compressive strain at room or high temperatures, or if the density reduction is not achieved, the hypothesis is falsified.

Own digest: Paper card. Question: What are the individual effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on the microstructure and mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and elevated-temperature performance) of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory high-entropy alloys?. System: Equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr and its five sub-alloys created by the subtraction method: HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi. Processing: Vacuum-arc melting of 99.9 wt.% (99.99 wt.% for Ti) pure elements stacked by melting point, re-melted at least four times, and solidified in a water-cool copper mold. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature, 800 °C, 1000 °C, 1200 °C, and 1400 °C; crosshead speed 0.36 mm/min (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); cylindrical samples 3.6 mm diameter x 6 mm height. Findings: HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy yield strength was 1512 MPa at room temperature and 556 MPa at 1200 °C.; HfMoTaTiZr (Nb removed) showed the highest room temperature yield strength of 1600 MPa
